turns.text: The previous story examined Wasserstein GAN. Now the camera turns to CycleGAN and a new question along the same timeline: If we take CycleGAN apart, which idea truly changed the direction of research?

CycleGAN made image translation possible when paired examples were unavailable. It used adversarial losses plus a cycle-consistency loss so translating from one domain and back would preserve content.
That sounds like a promising direction. What mechanism actually makes it work?
An image moves from domain A to domain B and back to A, with the cycle loss checking whether the original structure is recovered.

Experts generally treat CycleGAN as a landmark in unpaired translation and controllable visual synthesis. Its long-term legacy is the cycle-consistency idea used whenever paired supervision is expensive or unavailable.
Seen alongside Wasserstein GAN, CycleGAN reveals how the same technical question can echo across different eras.
